scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance commemorates a pivotal historical event in Central Java: the Treaty of Salatiga, enacted on 17 March 1757.
During the assembly to finalize the treaty, three rulers—Hamengkubuwana I, Pakubuwana III, and Mangkunegara I (Raden Mas Said, also known as Pangeran Samber Nyawa)—exhibited their military strength.
Mangkunegara I showcased multiple bregada (military units), among which was the Jurit Ampil, a unit composed exclusively of his garwa ampil (concubines) trained as soldiers.
on_screen: Map: Indonesia · Southeast Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The choreography conveys the complex concepts embedded in its title: 'jurit' (soldier), 'garwa ampil' (concubine of Mangkunegara I), and 'warastra' (bow and arrow).
It stands as a representation of female military discipline and royal sovereignty, reflecting on the historical unity and territorial negotiations established during the Salatiga Treaty of 1757.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Jurit Ampil Kridha Warastra is classified as a free-style dance, meaning it can be performed in groups, pairs, or solo.
It synthesizes classical Surakarta-style court dance with regional folk dance forms, borrowing extensively from the Prajuritan martial dance tradition.
Dancers manipulate traditional weaponry including bows and daggers while maintaining classical postures blended with military precision.
Watch for Jemparing manipulation, Cundrik stance.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Can be staged flexibly as a solo, in paired duels/partnerships, or as a synchronized group formation.

The instrumental layout includes the gender, kendhang, demung, saron, kenong, kempul, and gong.

The pulse is Javanese metric cycles (lancaran, srepeg, palaran).

scenes.title: The people
narration: The central historical figure is Raden Mas Said, titularly known as Mangkunegara I and famously referred to as Pangeran Samber Nyawa, who formed and commanded the original Jurit Ampil concubine troops.
The dance originates in the city of Salatiga in Central Java, drawing choreographic material from both the court styles of Surakarta and local Prajuritan folk martial dancing.

Beksan Jurit Ampil Kridha Warastra descends genealogically from the martial traditions of the Mangkunegaran court, merging Surakarta-style Javanese classical dance with vernacular Prajuritan soldier dances.

wardrobe.policy: the narrator wears the dance's traditional apparel, reconstructed meticulously and respectfully from the sources
wardrobe.from_sources: Performers wear female warrior attire. The hair is gathered in a small bun adorned with a golden crown. The core costume features a short-sleeved blue shirt embellished with gold trim, a belt, and a dodot wrapped over knee-length trousers. The weaponry kit includes the jemparing (bow and arrow set), composed of the gendewa (bow), nyenyep (arrow), and endhong (quiver), alongside a cundrik (dagger). Theatrical makeup is applied specifically to accentuate the bold expression and disciplined character of a royal soldier.
